subject: Agriculture
title: Synthetic Fertilizer
description: A quick win: understand Synthetic Fertilizer.

hook.text: By 1900, Europe was running out of natural fertilizer. Population growth was outpacing the soil.

buildup.text: Fritz Haber discovered how to pull nitrogen from air. Carl Bosch scaled it to industrial production.

discovery.text: The Haber-Bosch process turned limitless atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia-based fertilizer.

twist.text: The same process made explosives for World War I. Haber's invention fed billions and killed millions.

climax.text: Today, half the nitrogen in your body passed through a Haber-Bosch plant. It feeds 4 billion people.

punchline.text: One chemical reaction feeds half of humanity.

quiz.question: What does the Haber-Bosch process convert into fertilizer?

details.summary: Synthetic fertilizer, made possible by the Haber-Bosch process, converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia for crop nutrition. This topic covers the invention that feeds nearly half the world's population today and its profound environmental consequences.
details.whyItMatters: Without synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, Earth could only support about half its current population. It is both humanity's greatest agricultural achievement and a major source of pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
takeaways: The Haber-Bosch process was developed in 1909 and scaled up during World War I
Synthetic fertilizer is responsible for feeding roughly 4 billion people alive today
Excess fertilizer causes ocean dead zones, groundwater contamination, and nitrous oxide

faq.question: What is the Haber-Bosch process and why is it important?
faq.answer: The Haber-Bosch process combines atmospheric nitrogen with hydrogen under high temperature and pressure to produce ammonia for fertilizer. It enabled the massive yield increases that feed half the world's population today.

faq.question: What are the environmental costs of synthetic fertilizer?
faq.answer: Excess nitrogen runs off into waterways, causing algal blooms and oxygen-depleted dead zones. Fertilizer production requires significant fossil fuel energy, and soil microbes convert some applied nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.
